en: The Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha’s Vast and Great Enlightenment, Chapter on the Inconceivable Realm of the Buddha,
one fascicle.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Prajñā of Khotan during the Tang Dynasty.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Bhagavān was staying in the kingdom of Magadha, beneath the Bodhi tree, having attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and realized perfect enlightenment.
That Bodhi tree had deep and firm roots, well-planted in the earth like a sandalwood pillar.
Its trunk was tall and straight, with no branches or leaves on its sides; it was solid and perfectly rounded, and was named Aśvattha.
None of the birds are able to fly over it.
Its skin is fine and soft, its patterns like those of brocade; with immeasurable branches and twigs, they are exquisitely adorned and interspersed.

The surfaces of its leaves, both upper and lower, are adorned with a pure green; the veins are clearly visible, appearing like a deep azure-blue. The branches and leaves hang downward, perfectly complete all around.
Its flowers bloom in full splendor, most delightful to behold; their radiance shines brilliantly and their fragrance is exquisitely sweet.
Their roots, stems, and other parts manifest in various colors, endowed with every excellence, like Mount Sumeru.
Its lower part was magnificently adorned like the Nandana Grove; its radiance and fragrance extended for one yojana, and at night it shone from afar like a great mass of fire.
The ground on all four sides is entirely level and even.
Upon it grows grass that is soft and luxuriant, its luster fresh and pure like peacock feathers; it possesses a wondrous fragrance that brings joy and delight to the heart.
Countless small trees surrounded it on all sides.
This king of Bodhi trees was so magnificently adorned that nothing could serve as a metaphor for its excellence, except perhaps for the Pārijātaka and the Pāṭala trees.
The Buddha sat beneath a tree, surrounded by a great assembly, dwelling in majestic dignity like the moon among the stars in the pure void of space.

At that time, Buddhas from as many Buddha-fields as there are atoms came each from their own lands to this place; desiring to adorn Vairocana and for the sake of the gathered multitude, they manifested themselves in the forms of bodhisattvas.
Their names were:

the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva, Gaganagañja Bodhisattva, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva, Vimalakīrti Bodhisattva, the two Bodhisattvas of Great Majestic Power who Perfectly Accomplish the Two Roots, Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin Bodhisattva, Ratnapāṇi Bodhisattva, Mahāmati Bodhisattva, and the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra, who served as the leaders; such a multitude as these all assembled there.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable thousands of koṭis of bodhisattvas who manifested in the forms of śrāvakas,
all of whom also assembled there. They were headed by such as Śāriputra, Subhūti, Maudgalyāyana, Rāhula, Kauṇḍinya, Mahākāśyapa, Upāli, Aniruddha, Khadiravanta, Ānanda, Devadatta, and Upananda.

All of them have long practiced the six pāramitās and are able to draw near to bodhi; for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, they manifest in the form of śrāvakas within this defiled buddha-field.

Furthermore, there were immeasurable thousands of bhikṣuṇīs, with Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī as their leader; for the sake of taming inferior sentient beings, although they manifested in female bodies, they possessed the karmic activities of men.

Furthermore, there were Śakra, Brahmā, the World-Protectors, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others—all of whom were extraordinary beings, none but bodhisattvas—and they had all come to assemble.
Why is this? Because those Buddhas possess secret dharmas, majestic power, supernormal faculties, samādhis, and miraculous transformations.
How, then, can a bodhisattva fully comprehend them?
Even regarding the Buddhas, whose majestic virtue and supernormal powers possess boundless strength, all phenomena are empty, yet their various powers are able to function.
How can sentient beings be able to fully understand this?
Just as a person sees various things in a dream, yet upon awakening sees nothing at all—just like the perceptions within that dream—so it is, so it is!
Because of the delusion of dreams, the perception of the essence of phenomena arises.
The Buddhas, being awakened, have nothing to perceive; through various profound and unobstructed categories, they benefit sentient beings, for they have attained accomplishment in subtle liberation.
And beneath that Bodhi tree, the Bhagavān sat with his body erect, entering a samādhi called "The Inconceivable Realm of the Buddha.
This samādhi was supremely excellent and vast.

By virtue of this samādhi, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, remain constantly in meditative absorption; they maintain such adornment even while speaking, eating, walking, and up until the time of their parinirvāṇa.
The Buddha, the Bhagavān, is like Sumeru, the king of mountains, beneath which stands the Pārijātaka tree with its wish-fulfilling jewel.
Within his pure thirty-two marks of a Great Man, all the Bhagavāns of every Buddha-field are universally manifested, like reflections in a pure, round mirror.
Within each and every secondary mark (*anuvyañjana*), all the practices originally performed by the Bodhisattva were fully manifested.

From the causal conditions of King Prabhāsa-rāja at the beginning, up until the ultimate stage of Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara, every single act of ascetic practice was revealed—namely, the ability to relinquish his head, eyes, hands, feet, and various limbs;
his wife, concubines, sons, and daughters; his slaves, servants, and attendants; as well as his high positions, palaces, and so forth.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Guṇakośa, whose various practices had not yet brought about perfect enlightenment, questioned Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, saying:
"O Son of the Buddha!
Regarding the samādhi in which the Tathāgata abides: what kind of samādhi is it?
Son of the Buddha!
How does he spontaneously manifest buddha-activities to liberate sentient beings within the buddha-fields of the ten directions?
"O Son of the Buddha!
What is the name of this samādhi?
Venerable One!"
"How is this samādhi realized?
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva replied: "Good son!"
"Listen attentively!
I shall now proclaim this matter for you.
Thereupon, the bodhisattvas gave rise to a mind of reverence, gazed up at the Honored One’s countenance, and, abiding in right mindfulness, spoke with one voice:
“Excellent, excellent, Guṇagañja!
Your question is most subtle; yet that venerable one is able to know all things.”

At that time, the great earth shook in six ways: namely, it moved, shook universally, and shook equally and universally; it trembled, trembled universally, and trembled equally and universally; it roared, roared universally, and roared equally and universally; it crashed, crashed universally, and crashed equally and universally; it swirled, swirled universally, and swirled equally and universally; it opened and closed, opening and closing above and below, opening and closing universally above and below, and opening and closing equally and universally above and below; it surged in the east and subsided in the west, and so on, even up to the center and the edges, all being likewise.
At that time, all sentient beings found temporary relief from all their sufferings and afflictions, and exquisite celestial flowers rained down.
Then, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva addressed Guṇakośa Bodhisattva, saying:
"O Son of the Buddha!
This samādhi is the bodhi of all Buddhas.
O Son of the Buddha!
This samādhi is named "the inconceivable realm of the Buddhas."
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, always abide here; having received their prediction from Dīpaṃkara Buddha, they immediately entered samādhi at that very moment.

From then until now, they have dwelt without effort, manifesting throughout a single hair-tip an infinite number of buddha-fields, even unto all the atoms contained within every buddha-field in all buddha-lands, universally appearing them all.

Or he may manifest birth in the Tuṣita Heaven; having passed away from there, he descends to be born, enters the womb, dwells in the womb, and emerges from the womb, whereupon he is able to take seven steps and proclaim:
"I shall forever be free from birth, old age, sickness, and death; that which was to be done has been accomplished."

In some instances he manifests dwelling in a palace; in others he manifests leaving the home life, practicing austerities, attaining perfect enlightenment, subduing the hosts of Māra, and turning the wheel of Dharma.
Or they may manifest remaining in the world for immeasurable eons, liberating sentient beings from all their suffering and afflictions, even manifesting entry into parinirvāṇa.
Within a single thought-moment, they are able to universally manifest all buddha-fields.
As for the aforementioned activities, within a single thought-moment they encompass all kalpas without increase or decrease, all being effortless.
Until the entire realm of sentient beings has attained liberation, they perform all Buddha-activities in every place at every single moment.
Within these buddha-fields, even at the tip of a single hair, he manifests immeasurable buddha-fields.

Thus, those Buddhas possess boundless modes of conduct (*īryāpatha*), yet these modes of conduct pervade all of space; there is not a single tip of a hair where no buddha-fields exist, nor is there a single tip of a hair where, moment by moment, they do not manifest *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

All Buddhas, from their birth and manifestation of perfect enlightenment until their final parinirvāṇa, universally manifest within even a single atom all Buddha-fields equal in number to the atoms of all Buddha-fields, exceeding that count by being immeasurable and boundless.

Each of those Blessed Ones manifests the conduct of a Buddha in the Tuṣita Heaven palace; they manifest the deliverance of immeasurable sentient beings, yet the Buddha-fields are not small and the atoms are not large.
Why is this? Because all phenomena are not solid, being like illusions and like mirages.
Thus, throughout the entirety of the realm of empty space, such immeasurable buddha-activities arise; moment by moment, they constantly bring benefit to sentient beings without even a brief rest.

For example, suppose this assembly of great bodhisattvas, numbering as many as the atoms in ten buddha-fields, were to dwell within a space of twelve yojanas in the land of Magadha, each remaining in place without obstructing the others.

"So it is, so it is! Within a single atom, there are accommodated immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* Buddha-fields; there are other Buddha-fields that face one another, or are turned away from one another, or are situated beside one another, or are contained within one another, and thus they extend and turn in succession without obstructing each other."
It is like a person in a dream who sees various things in a single location; although they are seen, because they are not real, they cannot constitute an obstruction. Just so, just so!
All these Buddha-fields are manifested solely through the transformations of the mind’s measure.

In some worlds, one sees the kalpa-fire burning; in others, it has already been consumed; in some, one sees winds arising; some are pure, while others are defiled. Even within those Buddha-fields where no Buddhas appear, the various classes of sentient beings perceive them differently according to their own respective karma.
It is so, it is so! There are immeasurable transformations.

For example, when hungry ghosts are oppressed by hunger and thirst, some may see water by the side of the Ganges River, while others see ashes, or see pus and blood, or see it filled with excrement and other impurities.
So it is, so it is!

Within their own buddha-fields, sentient beings may perceive them as defiled or as pure; they may perceive them as being present with a Buddha, or as having entered nirvana; they may perceive them preaching the Dharma within a great assembly, or hearing the Dharma of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), or hearing the extensive exposition of the *dānapāramitā*; they may see them wandering, or standing, or sitting, or eating; they may see them at the height of two men, or seven men, or one *yojana*, or a hundred *yojanas*, or a thousand *yojanas*; or they may see them radiating light like the rising sun, or like the full moon, perfectly bright in the sky—thus do various differences appear according to their respective karmic actions.
Some see [the Buddha] after a long time, entering parinirvāṇa; others do not even hear the names of the Buddhas.
It is like hungry ghosts who, by the side of a river, may see fierce fire, or see various other things, or see such [visions].

In such a great assembly of bodhisattvas, each [bodhisattva] perceives within their own buddha-field the Buddha-Bhagavān appearing in the form of a bodhisattva. Alternatively, they may see a certain buddha-field being consumed by the fires at the end of an eon, or already entirely incinerated; or they may see this buddha-field filled with the realm of sentient beings, where the Buddha manifests for their benefit. There are Bhagavāns who take various buddha-fields and cause them to appear as identical within a single buddha-field—just as one afflicted by a cataract, due to the condition of that cataract, cannot clearly perceive various forms.
"It is so, it is so! Because consciousness is conditioned by causes and conditions, one does not clearly perceive the various marks.
Thereupon, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva addressed Guṇākara, saying:
“O Son of the Buddha!
I shall now briefly explain this dharma of samādhi for you.

Within a single kṣaṇa, in all places—extending even to the end of empty space and the realm of sentient beings—there are immeasurable and boundless buddha-fields within the measure of a single hair-tip; within a single atom, there are buddha-fields equal in number to the atoms of the entire dharma-realm. In each and every one of these buddha-fields, there are exceedingly many modes of conduct.”

Just as in a single moment, for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, there are as many deeds as there are atoms in ten Buddha-fields; so too, in every thought-moment, in all places, and for all sentient beings until they have attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, these acts of benefit shall never cease.

Such was his deportment; and likewise, the second, third, fourth, and fifth [Buddhas], up to all the Buddhas throughout the ten directions—immeasurable and boundless in their majestic virtue and power—were also exactly like this.

At that time, having heard this teaching, the Bodhisattva Guṇakośa clearly understood and thoroughly penetrated this treasury of samādhi; he entered the inconceivable realm of all Buddhas, awakened to the supernatural powers and majestic might of all the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, and by means of those various powers, skillfully tamed immeasurable sentient beings right there.

There were a hundred Ganges-sands of bodhisattvas who, regarding the dharmas of samādhi, had various realizations; some had attained the stage of patience (*kṣānti*), while others had realized the various stages (*bhūmi*).
Among them were bodhisattva-mahāsattvas such as Avalokiteśvara, who were like jars already filled with water placed in the rain, which could not accommodate even a single drop more.

So it is, so it is! The sublime practices performed by the assembly of Bodhisattvas dwelling in the tenth stage have all been brought to perfection. For a long time they have manifested Buddha-activities within this samādhi; they are able to condense immeasurable eons into a single kṣaṇa, and to condense immeasurable lands into a single atom. Thus, in a single thought-moment, they pervade all Buddha-fields, spontaneously liberating immeasurable sentient beings.

At that time, the Bhagavān dwelt in samādhi and emitted from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows a light named "Able to Arouse"; its radiance shone forth, illuminating those who practice with effort.
Although the assembly of bodhisattvas had not yet attained awakening within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), by virtue of being touched by the light, they were able to see all buddha-fields.

At that very moment, immeasurable buddha-fields—occupying spaces as minute as atoms or the tips of hairs—manifested throughout the entirety of space, appearing like mustard seeds filling a vessel of lapis lazuli.

"So it is, so it is! Within a single infinitesimal fraction of a mote of dust, one sees the Buddha-Bhagavāns of all Buddha-lands; within the body of a single Tathāgata, the physical forms of all Tathāgatas appear."

Each and every Tathāgata possesses immeasurable names; within a single kṣaṇa, in each and every Buddha-field, for the sake of benefiting each and every sentient being, they spontaneously manifest this *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, just as when a wish-fulfilling jewel is placed atop a high banner, it naturally rains down various kinds of precious treasures according to the needs of all sentient beings.
So it is, so it is! All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas bring immeasurable sentient beings to spontaneous liberation.
Why is this? Because all realms of existence are not solid, being like illusions and like mirages.
Thus, within these buddha-fields, sentient beings pass from one to another without mutual obstruction.

Just as one who manifests supernatural powers encounters no obstruction whatsoever from mountains, rivers, rocks, or walls, so too do these bodhisattvas, beholding the majestic power of those Buddhas, each appear before all the Buddhas in every Buddha-field. In a single kṣaṇa, they make various offerings at the site of each and every Tathāgata for one kalpa, or two kalpas, or three kalpas, or a hundred kalpas, or a thousand kalpas, or for a single kṣaṇa, or for a single muhūrta.

In the presence of the Tathāgatas, they hear the exposition of the pāramitās, or hear dhāraṇīs, or hear the teachings on the various stages (bhūmis); they witness the supernatural transformations and miraculous powers of the Tathāgatas, such as the entry of all kalpas into a single kṣaṇa, and thus conceive the thought that these are difficult to encounter.
How is it that the Tathāgata possesses such majestic power?

Within a single thought-moment, he manifests immeasurable eons; and for the sake of generating roots of goodness in us, he extensively expounds this mass of merits, as well as the inconceivable Buddha-realm samādhi cultivated over immeasurable eons, awakening us to such power and such majesty.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Guṇakośa asked the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra:
"Venerable One!
By what merit does one realize this samādhi?"
How does one cultivate wisdom?
How does one practice giving?
How does one maintain ethical discipline?
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva addressed him, saying:
"O Son of the Buddha!

Throughout all the pure and perfect buddha-fields in the ten directions, among all classes of sentient beings, immeasurable buddha-activities are manifested. These bodhisattvas accumulate various roots of merit and virtue, constantly and without interruption making offerings to the Buddha, making offerings to the Dharma, making offerings to the Sangha, and filially supporting their parents."

All those who are impoverished, suffering, solitary, or begging for alms, the Bodhisattva should compassionately embrace; even his own flesh and blood should be given away as appropriate, without giving rise to stinginess or parsimony.

Why is this? Because those who make offerings to the Buddha possess exceedingly great merit; such sentient beings will experience supreme and wondrous bliss and shall swiftly realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

As for the method of making offerings, it gives rise to all roots of goodness and causes wisdom to increase; because one shall attain awakening and mastery over phenomena, one is able to correctly understand all dharmas.
One who makes offerings to the Saṅgha plants various roots of goodness, whereby their immeasurable provisions increase and flourish.

By this means, until they attain Buddhahood, the Bodhisattva shall reflect upon repaying the kindness shown by those to whom they have been filial—whether it be their parents or their venerable Upādhyāyas—or others from whom they have received grace throughout the cycle of birth and death, ensuring that such kindness grows manifold.

Why is this? Because among the classes of sentient beings, those who recognize kindness and repay it—even when they commit sinful karma within the cycle of birth and death—will never lose those roots of goodness.
Therefore, all Tathāgatas constantly praise the repayment of kindness and reproach all those who are ungrateful.
How does a bodhisattva firmly accomplish all roots of goodness?

This refers to those who are impoverished, solitary, and so forth; toward them, one increases and expands great compassion and, through the methods of the means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), receives them.
When a Bodhisattva’s bodhicitta is manifest, they obtain these three kinds of fields: those with merit, those who recognize kindness, and those who possess compassion.

The Tathāgata has already explained the activities to be performed by all bodhisattvas: they should remain awakened, planting various roots of goodness in each and every field, making them vast, sublime, and fully perfected.
"Furthermore, Guṇagañja!
All bodhisattvas should extensively plant the seeds so that the sprouts of virtue may gradually grow.

This samādhi is the master of enlightenment; one should first plant these seeds before a Buddha or an image, making offerings with various requisites such as flower garlands, burning incense, unguents, powdered incense, song, dance, and music.
One should then reflect in this way:

"As previously stated, throughout all places—within the tips of the hairs and even within the most minute atoms of all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones—I shall perceive the majestic power of the Buddhas and the assemblies of the great multitudes of Bodhisattvas and others. Toward them, with a pure mind and with equanimity, I shall bring them to mind and perform offerings."

That is to say, the dharma-nature of one Tathāgata is the very dharma-nature of all Tathāgatas; if I make offerings to one Tathāgata, I have thereby made offerings to all Tathāgatas, and the same applies to making offerings at the abodes of each and every Tathāgata throughout immeasurable kalpas.
"Even to the point that many eons enter into a single kṣaṇa through the Buddha’s spiritual power, they develop profound faith and understanding.
Thus, those bodhisattvas plant seeds and attain the samādhi of the vast and inconceivable realm of the Buddhas.

Good sons and good daughters should daily perform such offerings before all the Buddhas, the Bhagavans; even a single joining of the palms will cause the sprouts of the seed of the Samādhi of Increasing Growth to flourish and expand, which should be watered with the nectar of ethical discipline (*śīla*), wisdom, and sublime vows.

Furthermore, bodhisattvas should practice giving in this manner: they must not discriminate between those who uphold the precepts and those who break them, nor between those they love and those they hate, nor between the poor and the wealthy. Indeed, even when the wealthy have no need for anything, one who is able to give to them gains benefit for themselves.
One should give rise to this sublime vow of equanimity:
"I shall certainly become a Buddha and deliver all sentient beings.

In every single moment, within every atom of space throughout all Buddha-fields, I shall individually accomplish [enlightenment]; even within as many fields as there are atoms in all Buddha-fields, and within each and every one of those atoms, I shall turn the wheel of the True Dharma."

Now, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Vairocana, is able within a single kṣaṇa to encompass all kalpas; spontaneously, in each and every buddha-field, I shall manifest immeasurable modes of deportment.

In every posture, throughout as many Buddha-fields as there are atoms, may all such sentient beings be liberated from suffering, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, even unto the end of the realm of space and the realm of sentient beings.

Furthermore, bodhisattvas should maintain pure ethical discipline; toward sentient beings who have broken their precepts, they should give rise to compassion and provide protection, rather than feeling aversion or abandoning them.
Then Samantabhadra Bodhisattva addressed Guṇakośa, saying:
"Son of the Buddha!
Regarding what you have asked, how does one cultivate prajñā?"
You should listen attentively; I shall explain it for you.

If there are those who seek unsurpassed bodhi and desire to realize this samādhi, they should distance themselves from false actions, harsh speech, and defiled intentions; they should give rise to a pure mind and embrace all beings with great compassion.

One should go into the vihāra and behold a most rare and wondrous image of the Buddha, standing firm and unmoving, its body adorned with gold leaf or fashioned entirely of pure gold. It is complete with all the marks and its limbs are full; within the halo are immeasurable Buddhas, beautifully arrayed and interspersed, sitting in the vajraparyaṅka posture and absorbed in samādhi.
Immediately before the image, one should pay respectful homage and reflect in this way:
"I have heard that all the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, currently existing throughout the ten directions,

are infinite and immeasurable— namely, Tathāgata Sarvārthasiddha, Tathāgata Amitāyus, Tathāgata Ratnaketu, Tathāgata Akṣobhya, Tathāgata Vairocana, Tathāgata Ratnacandra, Tathāgata Ratnasūrya, and so forth— and toward them I feel vast faith, joy, and reverence."
Furthermore, one should form this thought:
"I shall give rise to profound respect for this Tathāgata; until he naturally appears before me, I shall carefully observe him in all places."

Reflecting thus, he went to a secluded place and, with right mindfulness, focused his attention on what was near at hand—extending no further than the length of one arm—concentrating his recollection so as not to let it be lost;
if he were to forget anything, he should go back and observe it again.

When observing in this manner, one should give rise to a mind of reverence and conceive of them as being the manifest Buddha; one should not regard them as mere physical images. In this way, one will naturally behold the Buddhas face-to-face.

In that place, one should perform offerings with various requisites such as ointments, powdered incense, burning incense, and flower garlands, while circumambulating to the right. By maintaining this practice with every thought, the Buddha Bhagavān will naturally appear before one; because he can see all, hear all, and fully comprehend all thoughts and so forth, one should repeatedly and decisively grasp his marks and then go to a secluded place, never losing the mental recollection.
If there are those with merit who practice with diligent application during the twenty-one days, they will swiftly manifest before them and be able to see the Buddhas.
However, those who have committed sinful karmic actions in previous lives—such persons will not be able to see them.
If there is a desire [for enlightenment], one should arouse diligence, practice with valor, and observe with determination. Why is this?
Because by means of a single object, the mind is tamed; through such earnest and focused application, the provisions for awakening will all be accomplished.

If one is overcome by excessive torpor, indolence, and negligence, one will naturally fail to attain liberation in this way; how much less could one liberate all sentient beings from their suffering and afflictions?
This is like the great earth; it is truly a heavy burden.
If one is thus [burdened], one will also be unable to apply oneself with diligent cultivation to the direct path to enlightenment.
It is, for example, as if a person were to drink a single handful of water from the great ocean; they would have thereby drunk all the waters of every river in Jambudvīpa. Even so, even so!
If one cultivates the ocean of bodhi, all samādhis, all patiences (kṣānti), all stages (bhūmi), and all dhāraṇīs have already been cultivated.
Therefore, one should always be diligent and courageous, remaining far removed from negligence; by reflecting in this way, the vision of all Buddhas will naturally manifest before one.
"If you have already seen it, you should reflect in this way: 'Is that which is seen the Tathāgata,
or is it a physical image?'"
If one awakens to this presence of the Tathāgata, one should immediately kneel with palms joined before the Buddha and recollect as previously described:
"By virtue of the majestic power of all Buddhas, and through their great majesty and great compassion, they have now appeared before me."
"If you are able to pose a question, you should immediately request, saying:
'I only pray that the World-Honored One will expound for me the Dharma of the Great Samādhi of the Inconceivable Realm of the Buddha.'"
"Do not give rise to doubt or hesitation regarding this.
Whatever is taught therein, form a mind of certainty;
if you hear it, you will achieve complete perfection in that very place."
If, due to obstacles from past karma, one is unable to make this request, one should immediately perform various observations such as these:
"All phenomena are like dew, like cataracts, like illusions, like mirages, and like reflections;
likewise, all Buddhas are like space, equal by nature, neither illusion nor dream."

However, one should understand that all phenomena are like illusions and like dreams; through wisdom and compassion, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has appeared. Now, he should radiate the light of great compassion for me, so that all my suffering and affliction may be completely extinguished.
Furthermore, one should contemplate and observe the subtle nature of emptiness in this way.

At that time, the World-Honored One emitted a great radiance from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows; the light was named Blue Flame. It touched the crown of his head, whereby all suffering and affliction were entirely extinguished. He immediately attained a dharma therein called Vairocana-Endurance, and was able to awaken to various samādhis.
On the seventh night, the Buddha Bhagavān appeared before him in a dream and bestowed upon him the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
If one understands it thus—that this is a mere image—one should then contemplate all Tathāgatas and all sentient beings as being like the seen image, such that no substantial reality can be found.
"So it is, so it is! All Tathāgatas are like illusions, like transformations, like dreams, like mirages; they are naturally thus.
To behold a Tathāgata face-to-face is like seeing something in a dream; none of these are truly existent."

So it is, so it is! All Tathāgatas are not born yet are born, do not perish yet perish; they differ from all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), and their *dharmatā* is profoundly deep. They cannot be spoken by speech, they go though not going, they come though not coming, they are not what consciousness cognizes, and they are not the notion of a self, nor the notion of a life-principle, nor the notion of a sentient being, nor the notion of a nourisher, nor the notion of a person (*pudgala*), nor the notion of a consumer. They are neither the aggregates (*skandha*) nor non-aggregates, yet they possess the semblance of aggregates. The eighteen elements (*dhātu*) and twelve bases (*āyatana*) are ultimately and entirely non-existent, yet they are not different from them.

Because all Buddhas and all dharmas are equal and identical, sharing the same principle—like a mirage and so forth—all sentient beings and all Tathāgatas, as well as all Buddha-fields, do not depart from conceptualization (*saṃjñā*).

Such conceptualization manifests, and consciousness (*vijñāna*) takes form (*rūpa*) as its object; such is their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), which ultimately has no arising. When the consciousness of a Tathāgata ceases, it is therefore distinct from form.

One should observe and understand that if all phenomena are not separate from perception, then the Tathāgata is known as being without distinction even in the measure of a hair-tip, just like space, perfectly equal and uniform.
If I engage in conceptual discrimination, the Buddha appears before me; if there is no conceptual discrimination, nothing at all is seen.
One can conceive of a Buddha, yet apart from such conception, there is none;
likewise, all phenomena within the triple world do not exist apart from the mind.

If one can thoroughly understand that all Buddhas and the nature of all phenomena are merely the measure of mind, one will attain the Patience of Accordance or realize the Stage of Joy; then, upon casting off this body in another life, one will swiftly be born in the World of Wonderful Joy, or in the Pure Buddha-land of Ultimate Bliss, where one constantly beholds the Tathāgata and personally receives his offerings.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Guṇakośa addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra, saying:
"O Son of the Buddha!
If there are sentient beings who hear this Dharma-gate and receive, uphold, read, recite, copy, and extensively expound it, how much merit will they obtain?"
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva addressed Guṇakośa, saying:
"Good son, listen attentively!

As for the measure of merit produced by this, it is like a person who gathers all sentient beings of the three realms and causes them to be liberated from birth and death, attaining the fruit of arhatship."

Furthermore, toward that object, they give rise to pure intentions and a mind free from feverish affliction; for a hundred kalpas, they provide offerings of various requisites such as clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal elixirs.
After he has entered parinirvāṇa, if one erects a stūpa made of the seven precious substances to pay him respect and make offerings, the merit thereof is exceedingly great.

If there are sentient beings who hear this Dharma-gate and give rise to faith and reverence, and do not slander it, and furthermore practice the pure conduct (brahmacarya) for a hundred kalpas, cultivate patience for a hundred kalpas, exert diligence for a hundred kalpas, and cultivate meditative concentration (dhyāna) for a hundred kalpas, the mass of merit they produce will be limitless.

"If there should be another person who, upon hearing this Dharma-gate, gives rise to faith and reverence and is able to correctly receive and uphold it, they will swiftly attain Buddhahood; their merit shall exceed that of the former.
At that time, the Buddhas, the Bhagavāns, within all Buddha-lands of the ten directions, all manifested their bodies and praised Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
O Son of the Buddha!
It is so, it is so! It is just as you have said.

Thereupon, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni emitted rays of light of immeasurable colors from his face, illuminating the three realms and raining down various exquisite flowers. Thus, musical instruments played spontaneously without being struck, producing subtle and wondrous sounds that gladdened the heart.
At that time, the great earth trembled subtly, and from within the radiance, immeasurable sublime verses were proclaimed:
"If one hears this Dharma with a pure mind, One shall attain the various stages, concentrations, and dhāraṇīs,
As well as mastery over patience and wondrous supernormal powers, And swiftly realize the fruit of unsurpassed bodhi."
In the future, you shall be able to turn the wheel of Dharma, just as the Great Sages of the past;
within a single kṣaṇa, you will encompass many kalpas, and within a single atom, you will manifest myriad lands.
Immeasurable sentient beings fill the three realms; within them, the heedless undergo various sufferings, bound by evil views and lost from the right path.
In every thought-moment, deliver them all so that no effort is in vain.

When the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra spoke this Dharma-gate, all the sufferings and afflictions of a thousand koṭis of devas and humans were completely liberated, and they attained non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra has already thoroughly mastered this Dharma-gate and realized it directly before him.

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Guṇakośa, along with all the bodhisattvas, devas, humans, gandharvas, asuras, and all others in the world, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
The Chapter on the Inconceivable Realm of the Buddha from the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Great Vaipulya.
